chapters.name: Flexibility, Core, and Balance Technique
chapters.summary: How to teach foam rolling, stretching, core, and balance exercises, and how to make them easier or harder.
keyPoints: Self-myofascial release (foam rolling) applies pressure to tight or tender tissue.
Static stretching holds a position; dynamic stretching uses controlled movement.
A stabilization exercise keeps the spine still, like a plank.
Balance gets harder with a smaller base of support or a less stable surface.

chapters.name: Resistance and Cardio Technique
chapters.summary: Proper setup, tempo, breathing, and progressions for resistance and cardio exercises.
keyPoints: Tempo lists lowering, pause, then lifting. A 4/2/1 tempo is slow and controlled.
Breathe out during the effort and in while lowering.
A regression makes an exercise easier; a progression makes it harder.
Keep a neutral spine in a hip hinge and pull the shoulder blades back in a row.

chapters.name: Cueing, Spotting, and Safety
chapters.summary: How to coach with visual, auditory, and touch cues, spot lifts, and stop unsafe exercise.
keyPoints: Visual cues are shown, auditory cues are spoken, and kinesthetic cues use touch.
A spotter stays close to the bar and the client's wrists on a bench press.
Sharp pain means stop the exercise and check the client.
End a set when technique breaks down.

chapters.name: The OPT Model and Its Phases
chapters.summary: The five phases of the Optimum Performance Training (OPT) model and who should use each.
keyPoints: The OPT model has 5 phases in 3 levels: stabilization, strength, and power.
Phase 1 is Stabilization Endurance and suits most beginners.
Phase 3 builds muscle size; Phase 4 builds maximal strength with 1 to 5 reps and long rests.
Phase 5 pairs a strength exercise with a power exercise.

chapters.name: Acute Variables and Progression
chapters.summary: The training choices a trainer controls and the principles that guide how the body adapts.
keyPoints: Acute variables include reps, sets, intensity, tempo, rest, and exercise selection.
Progressive overload gradually raises the demands of training.
The SAID principle says the body adapts to the specific demands placed on it.
The general adaptation syndrome has alarm, resistance development, and exhaustion stages.

chapters.name: Cardio and Flexibility Programming
chapters.summary: Basic cardio and flexibility recommendations and how to set intensity.
keyPoints: Adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week.
Muscle-strengthening activity is recommended on 2 or more days a week.
Stage I cardio builds an aerobic base.
Corrective flexibility order: inhibit, lengthen, activate, integrate.

chapters.name: Health Screening and Client Intake
chapters.summary: Collecting health history and screening clients before exercise.
keyPoints: The PAR-Q+ screens readiness for physical activity.
Medical concerns need clearance from a healthcare provider.
Objective data is measured; subjective data is reported by the client.
Trainers gather information but do not diagnose.

chapters.name: Fitness Assessments
chapters.summary: Heart rate formulas, body size measures, and basic fitness tests.
keyPoints: Estimated maximum heart rate is 220 minus age.
Karvonen: (max HR - resting HR) x intensity + resting HR.
BMI is weight in kg divided by height in meters squared.
The Rockport walk test estimates aerobic fitness.

chapters.name: Movement and Posture Assessment
chapters.summary: Reading the overhead squat assessment and common posture patterns.
keyPoints: The overhead squat assessment looks for movement compensations.
Knees moving in: adductors and TFL overactive; gluteus medius underactive.
Low back arches: hip flexors overactive; glutes and deep core underactive.
Upper crossed syndrome means rounded shoulders and forward head.

subjects.name: Basic and Applied Sciences and Nutritional Concepts

chapters.name: Anatomy and Biomechanics
chapters.summary: Planes of motion, muscle roles, contractions, and the nervous system.
keyPoints: Sagittal plane: flexion and extension. Frontal plane: abduction and adduction. Transverse plane: rotation.
An agonist is the prime mover; an antagonist opposes it.
Eccentric means the muscle lengthens under tension.
Golgi tendon organs sense tension; muscle spindles sense length.

chapters.name: Exercise Physiology and Energy Systems
chapters.summary: How the heart, lungs, muscles, and energy systems respond to exercise.
keyPoints: ATP-PC fuels very short, maximal efforts.
Type I muscle fibers resist fatigue; Type II fibers produce more force.
Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume.
Aerobic training lowers resting heart rate.

chapters.name: Nutrition Basics
keyPoints: Carbohydrate and protein have 4 calories per gram; fat has 9.
Carbohydrate is the main fuel for higher-intensity exercise.
Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble.
One pound of body fat is commonly estimated at about 3,500 calories.

chapters.name: Communication and Rapport
chapters.summary: Listening, asking questions, giving feedback, and building trust.
keyPoints: Open-ended questions invite longer answers.
Active listening means paraphrasing and giving full attention.
Give one clear correction at a time.
Client-centered coaching means working with the client on goals.

chapters.name: Motivation and Behavior Change
chapters.summary: Goal setting, motivation, stages of change, and adherence.
keyPoints: SMART goals are specific, measurable, attainable, realistic, and time-bound.
Intrinsic motivation comes from within; extrinsic comes from rewards or pressure.
Stages of change: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance.
Find the barriers first when a client misses sessions.

chapters.name: Scope of Practice and Ethics
chapters.summary: What a trainer may and may not do, privacy, consent, and boundaries.
keyPoints: Trainers design exercise programs; they do not diagnose, treat, or prescribe medication.
Refer clients with ongoing pain to a healthcare professional.
Share only general nutrition information.
Keep client information private and keep professional boundaries.

chapters.name: Safety, Emergencies, and Business Practices
chapters.summary: Emergency response, liability, recertification, and facility safety.
keyPoints: For sudden cardiac arrest: call 911, start CPR, and use an AED.
An AED checks the heart rhythm and can deliver a shock.
Liability insurance helps protect the trainer from claims.
Clean spills and check equipment to keep the facility safe.
